q: You are about to boil water on the galley stove. What is the right order?
a: Strike the match first, then open the burner
o: Open the burner, then look for the matches
Open the burner, wait a moment, then light it
Open all the burners, then light the one you need
why: Have the flame ready first so no unburnt gas escapes — it sinks and collects in the bilge.

q: You have finished cooking dinner at anchor. Besides closing the burner knob, what do you do?
a: Turn the gas off at the solenoid or the bottle
o: Leave the bottle on, ready for breakfast
Just open a hatch to air the galley
Light the oven to burn off the spare gas
why: Shutting off at the source leaves no gas in the pipe to leak out overnight.

q: You come down the companionway and notice this. How do you deal with it?
a: No flames or switches, gas off, tell the skipper
o: Switch on the cabin fan to clear the smell
Light the stove to find where it leaks
Start the engine to run the blower
why: Bottled gas is heavier than air and pools low down — any spark can set it off.

fig.title: Below, at anchor
lines: Faint smell of gas in the saloon

q: The skipper asks you to cook pasta while the boat sails heeled in a lively sea. How do you set up?
a: Gimbals free, galley strap on, oilskin trousers on
o: Gimbals locked, galley strap on, shorts on
Gimbals locked, no strap, oilskin trousers on
Gimbals free, no strap, swimwear on
why: A swinging stove keeps pans level, the strap holds you, and clothing guards against scalds.

q: On your first day aboard, a guest asks what can go down the marine toilet. What do you tell them?
a: Only what you have eaten, plus toilet paper
o: Wet wipes, if the pack says 'flushable'
Anything small enough to fit the bowl
Paper towels and cotton pads as well
why: Marine heads block easily — everything else goes in the bin.

q: You have used the heads and pumped until the bowl looks clean. What do you do next?
a: Keep pumping a while longer to clear the pipe
o: Stop — a clean bowl means a clear pipe
Pour in some bleach and close the lid
Close the lid and pump again tomorrow
why: Waste still sits in the pipe after the bowl clears; extra strokes push it out to sea or the tank.

q: You need to use the heads. What do you do first?
a: Set the valve to the holding tank
o: Use it as it is — the tank is nearly empty
Use it, then pump extra sea water through
Use it as set — the outlet is well under water
why: In harbour, waste goes into the holding tank, never overboard.

q: Under sail the skipper asks you to close the toilet seacocks after each use. Why?
a: So sea water cannot siphon in and flood the boat
o: So smells from the tank stay out of the cabin
So the boat saves fresh water on passage
So the toilet pump wears out less quickly
why: When heeled, a toilet below the waterline can siphon sea water in through open seacocks.

q: How do you help the water last?
a: Turn the tap off while you soap and scrub
o: Run the tap until the water comes out warm
Rinse the deck with fresh water each day
Shower as usual — the tanks will refill
why: With no top-up, every litre counts: tap off while soaping, rinse sparingly.

q: You are at anchor overnight with no shore power and the engine off. How do you help the batteries?
a: Switch off lights and chargers nobody is using
o: Keep the fridge door open to cool the cabin
Charge all the phones and laptops overnight
Leave the saloon lights on until morning
why: With no charging, the house battery only holds what you save — switch off what you don't need.

q: The skipper says 'stow everything, we sail in ten minutes'. Your laptop is on the saloon table. What do you do?
a: Put it in a locker or wedge it so it can't move
o: Leave it — the table has a raised edge
Move it onto the chart table instead
Put it on a cockpit seat to keep an eye on it
why: When the boat heels, anything loose flies about — and breaks or hurts someone.

q: What do you do about the hatch?
a: Close it now, before water comes below
o: Leave it — it is cooler with air below
Close it halfway so some air still gets in
Close it only if a wave comes right in
why: Hatches and portholes stay shut under way — one wave through the forehatch soaks the cabin.

fig.title: Beating to windward
lines: Wind F5, spray coming over the bow
Forward cabin hatch open for air

q: The skipper warns of a lumpy crossing tomorrow, and you get seasick easily. What do you do?
a: Take a tablet before you sail and skip the wine
o: Take a tablet once you start to feel sick
Eat a big greasy breakfast to settle your stomach
Stay up late so you sleep through the crossing
why: Seasickness pills work best taken in advance; alcohol and tiredness make it worse.

q: Halfway across, you start to feel queasy. Where is the best place for you?
a: On deck in fresh air, watching the horizon
o: Below, reading to take your mind off it
In the forward cabin, lying down
At the chart table, checking the plotter
why: Fresh air and a steady horizon help; below decks, and above all forward, the motion is worst.

q: After a sail change at anchor, sheets and halyard tails lie in a tangle across the cockpit floor. What do you do?
a: Coil them and stow them clear of feet
o: Leave them — they will be needed tomorrow
Kick them under the cockpit table
Drop them over the side to trail
why: Loose lines trip people, and a line over the side can foul the propeller.

q: At anchor, a guest is about to drop an empty plastic bottle over the side. What do you tell them?
a: Keep it aboard and take it to the bins ashore
o: Fine, as long as it is filled so it sinks
Fine, if we are more than a mile offshore
Fine at night, when the beach is empty
why: Plastic never goes overboard: all rubbish stays aboard until you reach bins ashore.

q: Roughly how much can each person use per day?
a: About 11 litres
o: About 33 litres
About 66 litres
About 3.5 litres
why: 200 litres ÷ 6 people ÷ 3 days ≈ 11 litres each per day, cooking and washing included.

fig.title: Water check
lines: Three more days to the next marina

q: With no charging, roughly how long until that is used up?
a: About 17 hours
o: About 25 hours
About 50 hours
About 6 hours
why: 4 A + 2 A = 6 A; 100 Ah ÷ 6 A ≈ 17 hours.

fig.title: House battery
lines: Anchor light and cabin lights: 2 A

q: How do you spend the next three hours?
a: Go below and sleep, to be rested for midnight
o: Stay up with them and sleep after your watch
Have a strong coffee so you stay awake later
Keep the helm company until your watch
why: Off watch, sleep when you can — a tired watchkeeper misses things.

fig.title: Night passage
lines: 21:00 — the others chat in the cockpit

q: What is the problem?
a: The solenoid is off, so no gas reaches the stove
o: The bottle must be empty — change it now
The burner needs to stay open for longer
The gas locker lid has to be propped open
why: With the solenoid off no gas flows: close the burner, switch the solenoid on, then light again.

lines: Bottle valve in the gas locker: open
